_doc: Single source for SD-24's technology choices; see SD-08/stack.json for the format. `how` is spoken, so it carries no code.

stack.heading: Consensus groups: an etcd-class store
stack.title: A consensus-backed store: four groups of five replicas
stack.pick: etcd-class store, 4 groups × 5 replicas, one name in one group
stack.why: A lock needs a replicated record that survives losing a minority, an order for every change, leases that expire and an atomic set-if-absent. Its per-key revision is a ready-made fencing token.
stack.how: Writes go to the leader, are appended to a log, replicated and committed on a majority. A lease is an object with a time to live that keys attach to; when it expires the keys vanish. Acquire is one transaction: if the name does not exist, create it and attach the lease, else say who holds it. Every name lives in exactly one group, chosen by hash, so there are no cross-group transactions. Reads that must be fresh confirm leadership first.
stack.detail: The revision is stamped on every change and rises across the group; the token is that revision with the epoch in its top bits. Watches wake waiters in order.
rejected: One cache node, set if absent with expiry
Replication is asynchronous: the primary grants the lock and dies before the copy arrives, and the new primary grants it again.
A quorum of independent cache nodes
Safety rests on timing: a pause between acquire and use lets a second client assemble a majority. And it produces no token.
A relational row with select for update
A row lock lives as long as the connection: no lease, no token. Right when the resource is in the same database.
summary: Safety without timing; a revision as token
stack.course: theory/04 (replication and consistency) and theory/07 (correctness under failure)
drill: The leader of a group dies mid-acquire. Can two clients both be told they hold the name?

No. A grant commits only on a majority, and the new leader has every committed entry. A client that never saw the answer retries and learns the truth. The trap is a read from a follower that has not caught up.
committed on a majority; the new leader has every entry; fresh reads confirm leadership

stack.heading: Lock SDK: a library with a local deadline
stack.title: A library in the application: session, heartbeat, local deadline
stack.pick: JVM and Go libraries; a heartbeat every third of the lease
stack.why: The holder must stop on its own when it cannot prove it still holds the lock. That logic has to live in the process that does the work.
stack.how: The library opens a session and sends a heartbeat about every third of the lease, which is 3.3 seconds for a ten-second lease. It keeps a local deadline shorter than the lease. If the heartbeat cannot get through and the local deadline passes, it raises LockLost to the application, which must stop. The library never reuses a token after expiry.
stack.detail: A renewed lease is a new grant with a new token. The local deadline allows for the heartbeat period and the clock-rate error, not for a pause.
rejected: A thin client that only calls acquire
The application would have to build the heartbeat and the deadline itself, and every team would get it slightly wrong.
A sidecar process per host
One more process that can pause independently of the application, which is the failure we are guarding against.
drill: The application's thread pauses for forty seconds with a ten-second lease. What stops the stale write?
Nothing in the library can, since the whole process is paused. That is why the token exists: the resource rejects the stale write because a newer token has been seen.
the pause defeats any local check; the resource's token check is the guard

stack.heading: Gateway: stateless, with the slot map
stack.title: A stateless gateway: auth, quota, the slot map, a leader cache
stack.pick: Go service on Kubernetes, gRPC, three zones
stack.why: Clients should not know which group owns a name or who leads it. A stateless layer keeps that knowledge and can be restarted at will.
stack.how: The gateway authenticates the caller, applies a per-tenant quota, maps the name to its group with the slot map and forwards to the cached leader of that group. On a not-leader answer it refreshes the leader and retries once. It holds no lock state, so losing a gateway loses nothing but in-flight calls.
stack.detail: The operator console reaches the same gateway for force revoke, with its own role.
rejected: Clients talking to the groups directly
Every client library would carry the slot map and leader changes, and a rebalance would need a client release.
A shared layer-7 proxy
Leader routing is application knowledge; a generic proxy would round-robin onto followers.

stack.heading: Epoch store: a small durable counter
stack.title: A tiny replicated store for the epoch and the token floors
stack.pick: A three-replica strongly consistent store, outside the groups
stack.why: If every group were lost, tokens would restart from zero and go backwards. The epoch is the one number that must survive, so it lives somewhere else.
stack.how: The epoch sits in the top sixteen bits of every token, and the log index in the low forty-eight. It is read at group start and bumped only on a rebuild or a slot move, a handful of times a year. The store is itself replicated, three replicas across zones, and is written with a conditional update.
stack.detail: Token floors per slot are kept here too, so a rebuilt group seeds above every token ever issued.
rejected: Keep the epoch inside the groups
The failure it protects against is losing the groups. It must not share their fate.
A clock-derived epoch
A wall-clock epoch depends on clocks agreeing across a rebuild; a bad clock gives a smaller number.
drill: Every group is lost in a disaster. How do you restart without issuing a token an old holder could beat?
Bump the epoch in the epoch store, start the groups empty, seed the token floor above the old maximum, and wait one maximum lease before granting. Every new token exceeds every old one.
bump the epoch; start empty; wait out the longest lease

stack.heading: The check at the resource
stack.title: The token is checked where the write lands
stack.pick: A conditional write at the resource; a validating proxy where it cannot
stack.why: The lock service cannot stop a stale write; only the resource can, and only if the check and the write are one atomic step.
stack.how: Where the resource supports it, the token is the generation, version or entity tag, and the write is conditional on it: a SQL update where the stored token is at most mine, or a write-if-generation-matches. Where the resource is a partner API with no such primitive, a validating proxy keeps the highest token per resource in a consistent store and forwards only fresh calls. It fails closed.
stack.detail: The proxy's own step is a conditional update, so two concurrent holders cannot both pass.
rejected: A check in the application before the write
Two steps, and the pause lands between them. That is exactly the failure.
An idempotency key alone
Cheapest, and the right answer when the operation allows it. It does not help when the second write is a different, valid operation.
drill: The resource is a partner HTTP API with no conditional write. Where does the check go?
In a validating proxy that keeps the highest token seen per resource in a consistent store and rejects lower ones, failing closed. The proxy's step is itself a conditional update.
a proxy with a conditional update; fail closed

1: a paused holder wakes after expiry with no idea, and writes; only a token the resource checks can reject it.
2: Checking the token in the application
two steps, and the pause lands between them; the check must be atomic with the write.
3: A quorum of cache nodes for the lock
its safety rests on timing assumptions, and it issues no token.
4: Restoring the groups from a backup
the backup predates later grants, so tokens would go backwards; start empty with a higher epoch.
5: Every waiter polling the same name
a thundering herd at expiry; a watch wakes one waiter in order.
6: One global lock for a whole resource family
it makes one group the bottleneck for everything; split the name and keep one name in one group.
7: Alerting on whether the service is up
it can be up while grants miss their budget; measure acquire latency and token monotonicity.
